19251:
Hello everyone, I've been busy with work, but I've found a bit of time here and there to work on the Bally. I have some pictures below for you all.

I made the new keypad matrix out of the trace maker tape I have. Though my plans for thin traces was a joke, I was lucky to be able to cut the tape in half horizontally to get two traces out of each length of tape! But about half way through I realized I had plenty of room for this simple matrix, and I left the trace tape it's original width.

First I laid traces for the columns, 4 in all, and then I applied clear tape over them and laid the rows out in a new layer on top of the first. connecting all the keys and leading the traces up to the general front area. I then cut away part of the acrylic case and a hole in my keypad case for the wiring, which is not done yet.

I decided to trick-out the keypad keys with labels for MLM layout, the original calculator layout and also as a number pad for Bally Basic to compliment the full keyboard when I build it.

All peripherals are real with faux/simulated walnut wood grain except the keyboard which is real walnut wood with a faux/simulated keyboard.

Also, I don't think I showed this before, but my solution to all the cassette recorder cables and the inline switch was a mini corded extension that goes from the Basic cartridge, under the Bally hood and out the back to the inline switch in the rear of the cassette unit, with all the extra cording stuffed into the battery compartment. I cut a notch out of the battery compartment door so the cables could come out.
19252: I just thought I'd show you guys some shots of the Bally's general surroundings instead of just close-ups. Including the entire vintage computer layout I have, with the TRS-80 Coco 2 area shown as well, which I had been avoiding, since it's also a system project in the works and some of it's peripherals are in the shop atm, and it has no monitor as of yet. But at least you guys can see my entire computer "nook."

I might like a hi-res version of Bally Basic, it depends on how cumbersome I feel using MLM and doing cross-assembly. Which I'm not sure exactly what that entails (of course I know it means you do the coding on another computer), or if I'm stuck doing it on a PC, or if I might be able to use one of my other vintage computers for it*.

In any case, you were lamenting about no one else wanting to upgrade to hi-res machines. I will, eventually. The fact is I can't help myself. Upgrading and modding systems electronically and cosmetically is an obsessive-compulsive-disorder with me. I'm not normally OCD at all, just a high achiever who fancies himself a "Renaissance Man." But when it comes to vintage computers and consoles I am definitely and general audio/video electronics in general, I am very OCD, from everything needing to match in my systems and to have maximum upgrading and putting my artistic abilities to use in cosmetic restorations and custom builds. Definitely a perfectionist about it all too, and everything about my electronics has to be in complete symmetry and match, etc.

But until I'm done with my list of 1001 vintage electronic projects I didn't want to add to the unfinished list with what looks like, from my skimming your posts about the hi-res upgrade to be a large project, far more involved than adding a memory upgrade, real keyboard/pad and some spit and shine on the ol' gal until I'm done with at least the 6 or so upgrade and mod projects I'm in the middle of now, including the Bally for my part. But come next winter, I'm sure I'll do the hi-res upgrade during my slow season for my business. I'm back-logged with projects right now is what it is, and then I added the Coco 2 to the mix, and upon finally rewriting my Bally restoration blog on Atari Age which got me to finish it up, stalled due to a lack of a OEM PSU, though I had the parts to build my own for 2 years I ran out of time a few winters back and just never got back around to it until this past winter. And with all the help from you all and Allen especially, and he being a seller of Bally/Astrocades and upgrades, one thing lead to another...

* I actually do *technically* have another Z80 (well, *technically* 3) computer; I have two Indus GT disk drives for my Atari 800CX and a Indus GT clone, a CA-2001 drive for my 1200XL. These drives have Z80 processors and I've upgraded all three with what is known as the 'Ram Charger,' which is a 64K memory upgrade and CP/M OS. So I have basically 2 CP/M Z80 machines within my 2 Atari 8-bit systems. I could have 3 if I gave one of the Indus GT's for my 800CX to another 1200XL I have. It's in need of repair. But that is all just blustering at the mouth, 2 CP/M machines, one with two disk drives, is more than enough if there is an assembler I could use on CP/M and transfer over to the Bally Arcade.

End post.

New post

Ok, so instead of doing to email posts I decided to reply to Mister HR and give an update on my Bally in on email. So here is the update.

I finished wiring up for a keyboard and keypad on my Bally, though not nearly as neat at my first attempt that failed due to lack overhead room (I forgot about the cassette holder taking up space on the top case). But hopefully it gets the job done.*

Still using Dupont wiring and connectors so it can all be easily plugged and unplugged internally, though no more nice headers. I had to settle for single pin individual sockets to plug the new on-board keypad harness in, and since these pin sockets have posts, there was room to solder the pins of Dupont wires to the bottom of the posts, zig-zagging the wires and feathering them out to keep it low-profile. Then they connect to a 5 pin socket and 5 individual 1 pin sockets (I had to do this to avoid traces and ground planes on the bottom of the PCB) which connect to the 10-pin "test" edge connector on my Bally. I have two cables connected to the same plug, for both the keypad and for the keyboard when the parts arrive and I build it. I found a plug case for my keyboard connector, only needing slight modification.

I also finished hacking and wiring up my keypad, and it is finished and awaiting testing.

Which brings me around to fixing my Bally with the components I got for it so I can test the keypad. But, the one good tool I currently lack is a desoldering station or gun, which I intend to remedy soon, after my latest problem. You see, I started to desolder the regulators and transistors, but I still use a pump and soldering iron to desolder, along with some desoldering braid for final clean-up and those trouble pins and pads. But I'm out of desoldering braid, so I had to stop until I get more.

So, next month some time I'll be coming into a few grand extra cash and I have decided it is time for a good desoldering station, or maybe one of those guns...

Anyway, a few picks below again since I haven't had time to continue my blog yet. By the way, the mock-keyboard printout is actually what my keyboard will look like, except no back-lighting. I want it to look totally vintage and modern LED lighting isn't. Both my Atari's and peripherals all have internal lighting, but they are 80's computers, not 70's, and they aren't walnut wood motif. I will be adding a power led to the Bally, I think though.

The image shows the schematic of the custom data chip down to level of basic function blocks, PLAs, logic gates and transistors. The basic blocks itself could be found in the patent, too.
It is not the actual chipmask that was used to make the chips. It is more like a plan how the data chip could be build with regular electronic parts on a prototype pcb or bread board. As it was not uncommon back than to actually do this such a setup might have existed at some point.

I'm a game developer by trade. In my spare time i'm helping out at various projects with the aim to preserve old Arcade systems. One kind of these projects are PCBs that use modern components to replace the aging original game PCB. On the bucket list there is on such PCB for Midway 's cart rack based games like Gorf or Space Zap. In the case that this is not general known these games make use of the same 3 custom chips as the Astrocade. As such a PCB need to be plugged in a cabinet without any future (destructive) modification it is essential to get the video timing correct. This is generated by the custom data chip. Therefore I need to understand and replicate the behavior of this part on the chip.

Regarding an FPGA to replace only the chip. I i'm playing with this possibility, too. But as I i'm aware of failed attempts in the past I won't make any promises yet.

19289:
Thanks for the "Wow" compliment Adam on my 800CX. I have of course been restoring and upgrading both vintage computers and game consoles for about 20 years now. I've done several custom game console paint jobs over the years, though the 800CX is my first foray into custom painting a vintage computer.

I almost always want to go original with computers and restore them as close to original looks as closely as possible, though I might do some little things to make it look better with extra details like painting any raised text on the computer cases to make them easier to read and just give it that attention to detail that the computer company didn't bother with.

Consoles are easier (less to do) to custom paint as it's generally one case and a controller or two whereas computers have all the extra peripherals and so it all has to be custom painted to match if done properly. I originally restored my 800 to original condition and did a retro-bright to bring it back to original color, but it only lasted for about a year and yellowed again. I'd attempted it twice with my Sega Dreamcast with the same result of the yellowing returning, so I wasn't going to attempt it again on my 800. I'm sure it doesn't do the plastic any good either. In fact, whether from retro-bright or just from extreme plastic age, or both, my 800 and peripherals started cracking in areas or breaking entirely, like happened to the 800's cartridge door while I was doing the custom restoration. Body work was required and the only thing to hide it is paint.

But when I was just about to paint the 800 system as close as possible to original beige color, I remembered the mock-up of the IBM Personal Computer from when IBM was thinking of using the 800 hardware in their own PC's. The story goes that the deal was coming along in leaps and bounds until some IBM button-up executives visited Atari and saw all the hippies, many stoned, that worked at Atari and the entire culture that was very laid back and it turned them off trusting to go into business with Atari.

It is my understanding that it was IBM designers who actually came up with the case and colors of the IBM "Atari" PC. I fell in love it when I first saw the image of it above, and I decided it was the perfect opportunity to have as close as possible what might have been with a white Atari sold by IBM that I would have loved to own. I made my dream come true extrapolating from that image, adding my own unique twists and doing it across all the peripherals and controllers I own for the system.

19311:
I enjoyed watching the "The Bally Astrocade - A Professional Arcade in Your Home" video which was recorded at MGC2022 that was presented by Ethan Johnson and Kevin Bunch.  I have a few comments:

- I never would have thought to compare Mike White's 1980's Quadra cartoon to a crack-tro on an Amiga or Commodore 64, but I believe that Ethan is right.  It's not exactly the same, but the comparison is a good one.

- Maybe I have asked this question before, but, Kevin, where do you get the number of 28,000 Bally Professional consoles sold in 1978?  I really wish we knew the total number sold over the system's full lifetime.

- I wasn't aware that John Perkins worked on Project Nemo, along with Sewer Shark.  That's a fun tid-bit of information.

Kevin, did you get feedback at the show about the talk?  Did you get anyone who came forward and said, "Hey, I had the Bally Arcade as a kid!"

Keep on plugging the Astrocade in your Atari Archives videos, Kevin.  Someday, the Astrocade will make a full come back, Z-GRASS will be released (finally) and then those thousands of people who make Astrocade videos will occasionally drop the word Atari in a video now and then to keep those VCS fans happy.

Adam

P.S.  A "VCS" is a game console that was released in 1977 by a little-known company named Atari.

I enjoyed watching the session: MGC2022: The Bally Astrocade - A Professional Arcade in Your Home w/ Ethan Johnson & Kevin Bunch

Your session brought back many fond memories. Thank you for your kind words regarding ICBM Attack and Treasure Cove.

I chuckled at your comment about, "The light pen port that never got used for an actual light pen."
I actually hooked up a light pen to that port, and then used a light pen with the very first version of ICBM Attack. We (Spectre Systems) considered making a light pen instead of the joystick controller we ended up making, but chose not to because the light pen made it TOO easy to play ICBM Attack. That, and you had to have the system right in front of the TV so the cord for the light pen would reach the screen.

Anyway, it was fun watching your session. 😁
Thanks,
Brett

19321:
I doubt that a trip to the National Archives is necessary to find out information about:

1) 1980, Bally v JS&A. Suing their advertisers.
2) 1983, Magnavox v Bally. Ralph Baer/Bill Rusch patent infringement.
3) 1983, Astrocade bankruptcy.

Surely a trip to the local law library at a college campus will yield the same results.  This is how I've scanned suits that Paul Thacker has pointed out to us here (indeed, I think Paul has a document with MANY such suits; perhaps it already includes the ones above?).

Heck, even BallyAlley.com has scans of the 1984 bankruptcy paperwork:

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/Astrocade_Inc/pdf/Astrocade_Bankruptcy.pdf

The JS&A lawsuits are interesting, to say the least.  I've read some of the ones with the FCC.  They're fun reading material for a hardcore Bally enthusiast but will probably bore most others.

The librarians at these law libraries absolutely love to see their resources used by everyone and I strongly encourage people to take a trip there and just look at material that I suppose 99.9% of the population doesn't know exists.  Also, going in person is nearly essential to find some of this material, as even though it's public domain and it's in many college libraries, most of it isn't documented well online.  At least, that's what I've found over the last decade or so when I search for materials.  At the very least, talk to a librarian on the phone.  A simple five-minute phone call will teach you a lot about how the library system really works and how you much it differs from the way that you expect that it should work.

Adam

May/June 2022
Comments Compiled June 14, 2022
Version 1.0

These remarks were posted in the comments area for the video called "A Real Computer? Exploring the Bally Computer System aka Astrocade" by "8-Bit Show And Tell," which can be viewed here:

A Real Computer? Exploring the Bally Computer System aka Astrocade - YouTube<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69meAjHBAmU>
I was surprised to see the fairly obscure Bally Home Computer System video game console listed as a home computer in the 1979 Popular Science Buyer's Guide. ...
www.youtube.com
The video was posted on May 21, 2022.  The comments were made by Todd Johnson, Paul Thacker and Adam Trionfo.


TODD JOHNSON: I had programs published in the Arcadian. It actually worked just fine. There was a 48K expansion you could buy (I did) which you had to assemble using wirewrap and other tech of the time. The only issue I had was the controllers would eventually die. The potentiometers would fail and it became impossible to play the games whether in Bally BASIC or machine code. You could create your own machine code programs for the machine as well as BASIC. I got extremely proficient at typing on the calculator keyboard with overlay and could write a new game in about a day or two.


ADAM TRIONFO: Hey, Todd! I know your excellent Astrocade game. It's "Crown of Zeus" from November 1982. This game is probably the most RPG-like game on the Astrocade. It is for AstroBASIC only. It takes you to a dark decaying castle in the evil land of Sorom. You've been asked, as the best warrior in the land of Beekum, to retrieve the Crown of Zeus which the Scromites have stolen. The crown, when worn, gives the wearer the awesome ability to cause anything he or she wishes to vanish. Apparently the Scromites have not yet discovered the crown's powers. But as you hid in the forest outside the castle, you saw a troop of orcs from the warring land of Machor slip in through the front gate. They surely know the power of the crown and will have to be dealt with...

You can read more about Todd's game, here:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#CrownofZeusToddJohnsonAB

I'd love to see the AstroBASIC/Bally BASIC programming scene create some new games.


TODD JOHNSON: It has been such a long time. I had to draw the zone pretty much like the maps they made and then translate it into sort of an 'in-BASIC' database of x y z etc that were set to various numbers that let the program know which way it would let you move and what was in each room. The memory would not allow me to put the actual names of monsters etc in the game, so you had a piece of paper that listed each number and what it meant. Glad to see that part of it still lives on :)


PAUL THACKER: I'm a fan of the game as well, and love that you have a whole sci-fi backstory behind it. I've digitally archived many Astrocade tapes. Do you know that the other games in the Gibeleous series--The Rescue Of Catherine, Escape From Rantanam IV, and The Tower Of Machor--are considered lost media? Do you still have a copy of the games and instructions by any chance? You can find my contact info in my channel's About tab, or there's a link to our discussion group at the bottom of the Bally Alley homepage.


ADAM TRIONFO: I forgot to mention exactly what Paul mentions in his post here about your hopefully-not-lost follow-up to "Crown of Zeus." It would be great if those tapes could be recovered and archived. Also, in August of 2017, I made a video of your game, which you can watch here:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_uSGE2JYzl0
[https://i.ytimg.com/vi/_uSGE2JYzl0/maxresdefault.jpg]<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_uSGE2JYzl0>
The Crown of Zeus 1982 Bally Arcade / Astrocade game by Todd Johnson<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_uSGE2JYzl0>
The Crown of ZeusThe BASIC bonus game is The Crown of Zeus by Todd Johnson. This game appeared in the November 1982 Arcadian newsletter.The Crown of Zeus ins...
www.youtube.com
We played your game as part of the Astrocade high-score club that same month:

https://atariage.com/forums/topic/267047-hsc02-round-7-conan-the-barbarian-the-crown-of-zeus/

It's nice to see that you have fond memories of the Bally console/computer.


TODD JOHNSON: I'm afraid it will stay lost. Basically, the other games used the same main code but with a different piece of paper to correlate numbers with monsters. And a different set of values in the 'in-line database'. There were many things I wish I could have included in the games but couldn't with the less than 4K RAM. Much of that RAM was taken up by the BASIC module itself. So yup the game wasn't very forgiving (it was intended that you figure out how to plot the rooms and improve with each try) but I thought stating that in the instructions would be too much of a giveaway. And I freely admit it could have used some play testing by others! I especially wanted to add a few more lines to update the enemy strength, but they just weren't there.


PAUL THACKER: Thanks for the reply. We scanned a collection of papers from Bob Fabris, the Arcadian editor, and someone actually sent him a very detailed map they made of Crown Of Zeus.


ADAM TRIONFO: Thanks for letting us know that you don't have the game anymore. Perhaps the two sequels to "Crown of Zeus" exist on a tape someplace in the world. I suppose that you must have sold at least a few copies of the two sequels. Can you remember how many you sold? Paul refers to the maps that were made for your game. There are expertly made and I love the way that they both look.


TODD JOHNSON: It was strictly a hobby and not a business so very few were sold. I would say in the low teens :) One person kept asking for more, but I entered my last year in college and didn't have time.


END OF DOCUMENT

19349:
Hi Evie. I wanted to let you know that your desire to look into the possibility of designing a BackBit cartridge version for the Astrocade console is exciting news to me.

I'd like to ask you a few questions about your vision for the BackBit Astrocade version, here on I will designate as the BackBit AV. I thought it would be more appropriate if I broke down my questions (inquiries) into say 2 or 3 Astrocade discussion group postings. Actually, I only have a few questions.

I don't know if you have already spent time researching how the Astrocade functions. I thought I would start off posting a list of some FYI notes relevant to your vision of a BackBit AV.

FYI NOTES

The Astrocade motherboard schematic is included in the Bally Service Manual PA-1.
The Nutting Manual provides a detailed system description.
Both manuals are archived on the Bally Alley website.

The Astrocade motherboard operates only in the low-res graphics mode.

A system Reset forces the Z80 to begin executing instructions at the ROM address 0000H.

The 50 pin expansion is laid out as follows:
The odd pins 1, 3, 5 ... thru 49 are on the top of the motherboard, left to right as viewed from the front of the Astrocade.
Likewise, the even pins 2, 4, 6 ... thru 50 are on the bottom.

The SYSEN line (pin 50), when brought low (or switched to gnd) will disable the motherboard 8KB ROM (0000 - 1FFFH).

The CASEN line (pin 47) when low, will disable the cartridge chip select (active low CCS, 2000 - 3FFFH).

The active low BUZOFF line (pin 49) should be low when an expansion RAM or ROM is selected, so the Microcycler chip U10 is disabled (disconnected from the Z80 data bus).

All cartridge programs (up to 8KB at 2000 - 3FFFH) utilize a Sentry code 55H or C3H at 2000H.
The ROM power up routine checks for this Sentry to see if a cartridge is inserted in the Astrocade slot.

The 55H code indicates the cartridge program utilizes the Astrocade menu. A linked list of 6 bytes follows the 55H code at 2001 - 2006H for menu processing.

The C3H code, which is actually byte 1 of a Z80 three byte jump instruction, indicates the cartridge program does NOT utilize the menu. In this case, the Z80 will be instructed to jump to an address within the cartridge program.

Most cartridge programs execute calls to subroutines within the Astrocade ROM, which provides 64 user subroutines.

Calls must be made using the User Program Interface (UPI), which is located within the ROM at 0038H.

The Z80 is directed (jumps) to the UPI for subroutine call(s) processing when the Z80 executes a RST 38H instruction (opcode FFH).

The Nutting manual details the application of the UPI.

IMPORTANT

After a user selects an Astrocade program from the BackBIT AV menu for execution, the Astrocade ROM must enabled and made available so the program will execute without crashing.

If necessary, a short "switchover" routine can be copied somewhere at the bottom of the Astrocade screen RAM, then jumped to allowing the BackBIT OS to be disabled, the Astrocade ROM to be enabled followed by a Z80 jump to 0000H.

Bye.

Yes, it's already done. I already have a Z80 core, so much of the work was putting together the hardware and interfacing with the unique display chip. It took a bit longer than my work on the Mattel Aquarius, but considerably less time than the Magnavox Odyssey. Still, that's disregarding the 6 months of initial development time for the cartridge ;-) You can order extra adapters in the BackBit store.

I might do a video eventually, but I have a huge backlog of orders I have to build for the last 6 months since I've been waiting for chips to arrive. I should be able to start building on Monday.

It plugs into the expansion port on the back. There are multiple reasons for that, including the ability to provide RAM, BIOS upgrade, and the issue of actually being able to physically fit the cartridge.

Memory from 5000..FFFF is served as RAM. If you create a zero-byte BIN file, you can use the RAM expansion with any physical cassette of your choice. It's also possible to substitute the built-in BIOS ROM with any of your choice (not implemented in the interface just yet, but I did a test and it works great).

I'm a big Timex Sinclair fan as well, as that was my first ever computer, so definitely let me know when your next user group meeting is.

I have mixed feelings about the USB option. It's certainly something that can be available as an option, but it's problematic because cartridge won't turn off when the machine turns off, and that can send phantom power to the machine. If you have issues with your power supply from an extra 50-100mA on the 5V line, you're probably best off renovating your power supply anyway. 19387:
Good news guys! I got it working!!

got my Atari and Astrocade both working simultaneously with this setup:

Atari 2600 and Astrocade both use an Rf-coax adapter, then each line connects with a coax A/B switch that feeds an Rf booster (coax in/out) which feeds the VCR which converts to RCA out, using an RCA splitter to split two lines to two different HDMI up converter boxes, which then go HDMI out to my HDMI switchers. Whew! (Most convoluted setup ever!)

Whenever I want to play, I have to do the following: power on to selected device through surge protector switch, power on at unit, VCR on, tune to channel 3, HDMI switch box on at channel for that device, TV on, at input for each HDMI switcher, soundbar on, and toggle the coax A/B adapter to either Atari/Bally for either unit.

simple. :-P

On August 31, 2022, Adam Trionfo (that's me!) wrote, "I'm hoping it is information [about ZGRASS] that I have not seen yet, but maybe the information was also published elsewhere."

It turns out that the article isn't new; I've read it before now, but I never credited the source as "SIGGRAPH '78 Proceedings."  The librarian I talked to today at the information desk was VERY helpful and wrote me an email a couple of hours after I talked to her.  She said:

"I talked with ILL downtown and got a little more clarification on the unfilled. They think guessing on the library lenders’ responses, they probably don’t physically have it. However, they did find this link. It may not be the complete book, but the articles provided here seem to be free:"

https://dl.acm.org/doi/proceedings/10.1145/800248

She closed out by saying, "Hope this helps!"

Yes, it helps me!  Now I know the article is called:

BASIC Zgrass: A Sophisticated Graphics Language for the Bally Home Library Computer," by Tom DeFanti, Jay Fenton, and Nola Donato.  August 1978, pp 33-37.

The five-page pdf is available from the above link to read for free.  It's also available on my website, where it is credited with coming from: Computer Graphics, 12, no. 3, (August 1978): 33-37.

You can read it on BallyAlley.com, here:

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/zgrass/zgrass_docs/zgrass_basic.pdf

If ZGRASS interests you, then there is more general information and documentation about it here:

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/zgrass/zgrass_docs/zgrass_docs.html

19415:
I received mine this week as well and was just about to write a review, so
may as well tack it onto your related post, Adam. Mine is specific to Bally
testing this evening.

 

A Note About +5V Requirements

 

For the Bally adapter, the important point to keep in mind is that it
requires the external +5V feed, done through the light gun port. This is
equivalent to the way Lil White RAM gets its power or the original BASIC
adapter.

 

Evie includes a solderless pinout wire where one end has a gripper that can
carefully latch onto the +5V pin of the Bally light gun port, and the other
feeds into a female header on the Bally Adapter (the PCB is labeled clearly
in the corner "Power via LIGHT GUN").

 

Regardless of Bally variant, I'd generally recommend adding a hardwired plug
connector like Lil White RAM does for stability of the connection if you
have the means. This will ensure the wire won't accidentally come undone
from the Bally when running if it gets bumped, and that the connection will
remain steady at all times.

 

Thick 3 Pin Modification (BASIC Adapter Compatibility)

 

My Bally does not use that smaller 3-pin plug. Instead it uses the thicker
and offset internal pins, so the easiest solution is to use the original
BASIC adapter to feed into the Bally, and then feed the BackBit (or Lil
White RAM or Cassette Adapter) into that.

 

To get this working properly, I took an 18-20 gauge wire and soldered it
directly to the +5V on the BackBit Bally adapter where the pinout header is.
On the other end of the wire I added a Molex connector that matches the
original BASIC one and added a crimp connector pin, inserted into the +5V
hole. To be more precise, the components used to match this arrangement are:

 

*	Series 2139 - MOLEX 09-50-3031 PLUG & SOCKET HOUSING, RECEPTACLE,
3POS, 3.96MM - 5935-00-148-4250 (I clipped the extruded tabs off so that it
would fit within the BASIC adapter plugged into Bally)

 

*	Series 2478 - NSSP Molex 0008520072 08-52-0072 396 KK Crimp Contact
Terminal 2478 18-24 Awg

 

I completed this same exact procedure for my Lil White RAM so that I was
able to use that in the same manner with my Bally, easily swapping between
BASIC Cassette Loader and Lil White RAM (and now also BackBit) by just
swapping the Molex connector, but without ever having to disturb the BASIC
adapter plugged into the Bally light gun port.

 

SD Card

 

I have a lot of vanilla 4GB Micro SD cards from stock Android phones back in
the day. These have plenty of capacity for everything ever made for Bally
(when ROMs are only 2-8KB each) and many other 8-bit systems combined.
Easily formatted as FAT32 in Windows (if you exceed a 32GB card you may have
to use a third party formatting tool to retain FAT32).

 

I created a Bally folder on the drive and simply copied the TOSEC ROM set
from Adam into it. It gets inserted into the BackBit with the front of the
card facing the front of the BackBit. It is not a spring-loaded port so you
just push down until it stops, and then pull with slight force to remove.

 

The font size and Bally resolution only shows around 18-20 characters per
line, so it'd be in your best interest to rename the files so they don't get
cut off on screen.

 

Connection and Operation

 

Once all of this is done, BackBit connects to the Bally expansion slot and
the +5V to the light gun port. The expansion slot is a very snug fight so it
is easiest if you connect one side first and then the other, back and forth
slowly until secured. When you power it up, if all is working well the LED
will flash red briefly. You'll see the BackBit splash screen and then the
directory listing to navigate the SD card.

 

In this example, I found the "Bally" directory and pressed Trigger to enter
it. Up and down traverse the files individually, while left and right scan a
page at a time. Pressing trigger on any ROM will load that into memory as if
you've inserted a cartridge (or set the dip switches on the multicart).

 

To return back to the main list, you can simply press the red button the
BackBit! This is very convenient, for sure. The ROM images I tested worked
fine. There are other commands from the keypad that can get you into BackBit
settings and properties. Pressing '1' (Space button in BASIC) will enter the
options. You can scroll through those and press Tigger to alter an item, and
at the bottom it indicates other buttons to access different screens. Fast
Boot will remove the splash screen so it loads right to the listing. The
time can be erased by pressing CE on the keypad but I admit I didn't figure
out how to input other values but didn't investigate too much.

 

Powering off the Bally will power off the BackBit. It is always recommended
to power the Bally off before adding or removing the SD card or adapter.

 

BASIC and Machine Language Development

 

For BASIC applications, there is no cassette load or save ability built in
(PRG or WAV format files do not work, only programs converted to ROMs as BIN
files are directly runnable). This is where UltiMulti and Lil White RAM are
still very useful for the many BASIC programs out there since that combo
makes loading AstroBASIC / Blue Basic files easy including those requiring
extended RAM. You can of course launch the BASIC flavors from BackBit and
use them as normal, it's just not particularly beneficial compared to
UltiMulti if you have that already.

 

Evie previously noted in discussions that: "Memory from 5000..FFFF is served
as RAM. If you create a zero-byte BIN file, you can use the RAM expansion
with any physical cassette of your choice."

 

For machine language development and testing, this SD capability is
exceptionally helpful! Previous tests of custom Z80 programs on a physical
machine would require very cumbersome processes often including creating
special EPROM adapters, erasing and programming the binaries into EPROMs and
all that work. Now, you can compile the assembly into binary using your
favorite PC/Mac editor and toolset, and then just copy that binary onto the
SD card to test on the real thing.

 

This greatly motivates me to pursue more Z80 development on this platform,
whenever time may permit. In the screenshot you can see a simple "Hello
Bally Group" listing made from Z80 and copied to BackBit. Works great!

 

Conclusion

 

The BackBit is definitely a valuable modern toolset for quickly loading and
trying new and existing ROMs. I appreciate that affordable adapters exist
for so many platforms, including quite a few that otherwise lack an easy and
efficient SD solution. 

 

If you already have an SD/USB flash media solution for the platform, this is
probably not an essential tool but still comes with handy enhancements and a
very easy interface to navigate. On certain platforms there are other
benefits as well, I also got the Aquarius adapter that contains integrated
32K that would previously require a mini expander and cartridge. The concept
of nondestructive save/load states on supported platforms is also beneficial
(Bally gave the message 'unsupported' when attempting this).

 

Matt

19416:
Addendum: You also will want to upgrade the firmware when you receive yours.
I didn't realize mine was still on firmware version 1.3.3 and the latest is
1.4.3 release just this week. You can grab the firmware and official
documentation (general, not Bally specific) here:
http://backbit.io/downloads/

 

To upgrade firmware, you download the ZIP file and extract the update file
(bbpro.upg) to the root of your SD card. The next time you put it in the
BackBit and power on it will upgrade automatically. Reboot once to make sure
all is set.

 

My uncertainty of how to change the internal clock time in my original
review seems to have affected other platforms as well and was a firmware
bug. It is said to now be fixed for Intellivision but I still experience the
symptoms in Bally so I've reached out to Evie to make her aware. There's an
alternative way to update the date noted in the documentation involving
poking values to particular memory addresses, and those values will then be
saved on power off.

 

Have fun!

 

Matt

slowly until secured. When you power it up, if all is working well the LED
will flash red briefly. You'll see the BackBit splash screen and then the
directory listing to navigate the SD card.

 

In this example, I found the "Bally" directory and pressed Trigger to enter
it. Up and down traverse the files individually, while left and right scan a
page at a time. Pressing trigger on any ROM will load that into memory as if
you've inserted a cartridge (or set the dip switches on the multicart).

 

To return back to the main list, you can simply press the red button the
BackBit! This is very convenient, for sure. The ROM images I tested worked
fine. There are other commands from the keypad that can get you into BackBit
settings and properties. Pressing '1' (Space button in BASIC) will enter the
options. You can scroll through those and press Tigger to alter an item, and
at the bottom it indicates other buttons to access different screens. Fast
Boot will remove the splash screen so it loads right to the listing. The
time can be erased by pressing CE on the keypad but I admit I didn't figure
out how to input other values but didn't investigate too much.

 

Powering off the Bally will power off the BackBit. It is always recommended
to power the Bally off before adding or removing the SD card or adapter.

 

BASIC and Machine Language Development

 

For BASIC applications, there is no cassette load or save ability built in
(PRG or WAV format files do not work, only programs converted to ROMs as BIN
files are directly runnable). This is where UltiMulti and Lil White RAM are
still very useful for the many BASIC programs out there since that combo
makes loading AstroBASIC / Blue Basic files easy including those requiring
extended RAM. You can of course launch the BASIC flavors from BackBit and
use them as normal, it's just not particularly beneficial compared to
UltiMulti if you have that already.

 

Evie previously noted in discussions that: "Memory from 5000..FFFF is served
as RAM. If you create a zero-byte BIN file, you can use the RAM expansion
with any physical cassette of your choice."

 

For machine language development and testing, this SD capability is
exceptionally helpful! Previous tests of custom Z80 programs on a physical
machine would require very cumbersome processes often including creating
special EPROM adapters, erasing and programming the binaries into EPROMs and
all that work. Now, you can compile the assembly into binary using your
favorite PC/Mac editor and toolset, and then just copy that binary onto the
SD card to test on the real thing.

 

This greatly motivates me to pursue more Z80 development on this platform,
whenever time may permit. In the screenshot you can see a simple "Hello
Bally Group" listing made from Z80 and copied to BackBit. Works great!

 

Conclusion

 

The BackBit is definitely a valuable modern toolset for quickly loading and
trying new and existing ROMs. I appreciate that affordable adapters exist
for so many platforms, including quite a few that otherwise lack an easy and
efficient SD solution. 

 

If you already have an SD/USB flash media solution for the platform, this is
probably not an essential tool but still comes with handy enhancements and a
very easy interface to navigate. On certain platforms there are other
benefits as well, I also got the Aquarius adapter that contains integrated
32K that would previously require a mini expander and cartridge. The concept
of nondestructive save/load states on supported platforms is also beneficial
(Bally gave the message 'unsupported' when attempting this).

 

Matt

requires the external +5V feed, done through the light gun port. This is
equivalent to the way Lil White RAM gets its power or the original BASIC
adapter.

carefully latch onto the +5V pin of the Bally light gun port, and the other
feeds into a female header on the Bally Adapter (the PCB is labeled clearly
in the corner "Power via LIGHT GUN").

 

Regardless of Bally variant, I'd generally recommend adding a hardwired plug
connector like Lil White RAM does for stability of the connection if you
have the means. This will ensure the wire won't accidentally come undone
from the Bally when running if it gets bumped, and that the connection will
remain steady at all times.

3POS, 3.96MM - 5935-00-148-4250 (I clipped the extruded tabs off so that it
would fit within the BASIC adapter plugged into Bally)

Terminal 2478 18-24 Awg

to use a third party formatting tool to retain FAT32).

from Adam into it. It gets inserted into the BackBit with the front of the
card facing the front of the BackBit. It is not a spring-loaded port so you
just push down until it stops, and then pull with slight force to remove.

 

The font size and Bally resolution only shows around 18-20 characters per
line, so it'd be in your best interest to rename the files so they don't get

19432:
Jeremy wrote on September 21, 2022, "Pizza break! Lol, I haven't heard that one before."

When Ken Lill says, "Pizza Break," he is making a reference to "Nutting Manual."  This is a routine called, "PIZBRK" which is described as "Coffee Break, Black Out Screen, Wait For Key."  This is a subroutine that is part of the Bally's 8K on-board ROM, which is part of the Sentry routine.

Here is the full description of "PIZBRK" from the "Nutting Manual:"

This routine blacks out the screen and waits for either a key press or a trigger or a joystick change. This function should be called whenever a "hold until further notice"
is needed. All keys on the keypad are enabled. Interrupts are disabled on entry and enabled on exit. It is a good idea to reset any 60th of a second timers on exiting PIZBRK.

Now, let's REALLY get into the weeds!  For fun, I've clipped out the source code from the SENTRY routine.  Oh, Z80 assembly code; joy!

Included below is the sentry source code, included here for no good reason other than because it's available on BallyAlley.com, here:

https://ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/ml_source.html#AstrocadeOn-BoardROM

To put this code in context, you need to reference the "Nutting Manual:"

https://ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/ml_docs.html#NuttingManual

I'm glad this sort of information is available on BallyAlley.com, but it doesn't get used often, so I like to point it out once in a while.  Here ya go.  - Adam


  ; ****** SENTRY [SENse TRansition] routine
  ; Purpose:      TO WAIT FOR CHANGE OF PROGRAM STATUS
  ;               IN EITHER THE PORTS OR THE TIMER-COUNTERS.
  ; IN ADDITION IT CHECKS TIMOUT FOR LONG, PERIODS OF IN-
  ; ACTIVITY.
  ; ** IS VECTOR OUT FLAG SET??
MENTRY:
        LD      A,(SENFLG)
        CP      $AA
        JP      Z,STVECT        ; YES - JUMP OUT to cartridge
        LD      A,(TIMOUT)      ; CHECK IF TIME TO BLAKOUT
        OR      A
        JR      NZ,TTEST                ; (+$2b)
  ; ****** PIZza BReaK entry point
MPIZBK: XOR     A               ; TIME TO SHUT DOWN
        DI
        OUT     (VOLC),A        ; TURN OFF SOUNDS
        OUT     (VOLAB),A
        LD      BC,($08 SHL 8) + COLBX
PBLP:   OUT     (C),A           ; PAINT IT BLACK
        DJNZ    PBLP                    ; (-$04)
        LD      DE,AKEYS
        CALL    FINDL3          ; CALL STORE DE INTO CONTEXT RO
        CALL    TTEST           ; WAIT FOR SOMETHING TO HAPPEN
        INC     A
        JR      NZ,MPIZBK               ; (-$19)
        LD      (IY+CBA),$00
        EI
        LD      HL,(COLLST)     ; GET SAVED COLORS
  ; ****** COLors SET entry point
MCOLOR: LD      (COLLST),HL     ; SAVE COLORS FOR FUTURE
        LD      BC,$800 + COLBX
        OTIR                    ; RESET THE COLORS
        XOR     A
        RET

If your controllers are getting sloppy in the sockets, take a pair of pliers or channel-locks end squeeze the ends of the controller plugs. Don't squeeze them hard, just fairly firm. If you squeeze them too hard, you may not be able to get the plugs back in.
If you plan on reflowing the solder, male sure you have a GOOD solder. I prefer Kester 60/40. The thinner the better! Make sure you heat the solder and the pin until the solder flows and then just touch the new solder to the connection. Too much could short to another joint, and if it doesn't flow (turn to a liquid-like state) then your connection may end up being bad.

I've archived a commercial tape from WaveMakers--L.T. (Little Terrestrial). This is one of the rare attempts at a making a platformer on the system. Thanks to Nate Reeder for loaning this tape. I'd previously archived this program, including from the master tapes, but I hadn't seen this exact version before. And while the game itself doesn't seem any different from what I played before, there was in a fact a surprise--two bonus songs from Michael Peace. Riding White Horses was stuck in my head all day after I recorded it.

Complete files are here:

https://archive.org/details/l-t-little-terrestrial

L.T. (Little Terrestrial) is a program for the Astrocade game console published by WaveMakers (Michael Peace). A version of the program from the master tapes has previously been archived:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/wave_makers/L.T.%20(Little%20Terrestrial)%20(WaveMakers).zip

These files come from a commercially released tape. The tape label says copyright 1980, but the actual release date is 1982 as seen on the instructions and program title screen.

The game should be loaded into Astrovision BASIC (the version with the built in interface) with the command:

:INPUT; RUN

Included are scans of the tape and manual, raw recordings (which probably won't load), and digitally processed recordings that should work with either an original system or in MAME. Also included are two songs from Michael Peace put as a bonus on the tape, as he is also a musician.

Michael Peace released his Astrocade programs to the public domain on August 7, 2001:

https://ballyalley.com/faqs/astrocade_pd_faq.txt

Side 1 -- This version of the game has each player use their own joystick. There are two copies with no apparent differences. Following the program is an audio track from Micheal Peace, who is also a musician, "Riding White Horses". Micheal Peace also uploaded a different version of this song to YouTube on September 30, 2018.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q9-GVQJgKR8

Side 2 -- This version of the game has each player pass joystick #1. There are two copies with no apparent differences. Following the program is an audio track from Michael Peace, who is also a musician, "Now And Forever". Michael Peace also uploaded a slightly different version of this song to YouTube on July 28, 2019.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qp_V8Zdme6c

19452:
I’m not aware of any place RF shielding was documented, but I was not involved with manufacturing.

But… the RF shielding should be connected to ground somewhere, otherwise it is not very effective.
The shielding does not have to be soldered, but on some products it is. The shielding just needs to be touching a ground point somewhere so it grounds any signals the shielding catches.

The shielding is not as much for preventing signals from interfering with the game, but more to prevent noise from the game affecting other devices (TV, Radio, etc.).
That was a bigger problem when systems were analog. Today’s digital products are less affected by RF noise.

Well, unless it is an airplane, then not putting your phone in ‘airplane mode’ can crash the airplane.

(Not really. The real reason they have you put your phone in airplane mode is so you are not talking on your phone while they give the safety presentation.) 😁

Mike Peace's songs sound like they're firmly grounded in the mid-1960s.  As a musician himself, who is also influenced by this era of music, I'm curious what Chris++ thinks of these songs.  What era does he think inspired, for instance, "Riding White Horses:"

https://archive.org/details/l-t-little-terrestrial/audio/Michael+Peace+-+Riding+White+Horses+(from+L.T.+Side+1).wav

Since Mike had one-man-band performances (or as he called them "One Peace Band"), I guess this music was recorded on a multitrack system of his own.

I scanned-in an ad and picture from the early 1980s of Mike playing someplace-- it's on a flyer, here:

https://ballyalley.com/articles_and_news/One%20Peace%20Band/The%20Story%20of%20Mike%20Peace%20(One%20Peace%20Band).pdf

Here is the complete text from the article:

"The Story of Mike Peace (One Peace Band)

"Mike starred a 3 piece band back in 1964 and has performed in nightclubs, hotels, concert stages, and radio and television appearances. Also to his credit is a lot of recording studio work. He and his band have released 10-45's, 3-8-track tapes and 2 albums. Some of the engineering on these sessions was done by Mike himself. Using this experience Mike has set out on his own with recorded musical background as part of his accompaniment. When you hear Mike perform you hear him playing all the instruments. Mike records the drums, bass, piano, vocal harmonies etc. on a 4-track recorder, everything except his solo voice and guitar which he plays live in each performance. With all the instruments and voices behind him he sounds like a 5 or 6 man band, maybe more.

"Some of the instruments you'll hear Mike play are: guitar, bass, drums, harmonica, trumpet, xylophone, piano, organ, Casio keyboard, Astrocade music synthesizer, conduit tubing, bottles, jars, tin cans, bananas, oranges, and boxes. Also, you'll hear an amazing instrument which Mike plays live during his performance. It's called a Guitorgan, a Univox guitar with a Hammond B-3 organ built in. Mike can play the guitar or the built-in organ or both at the same time. Hearing all of this coming from one guy will amaze you all to heck!

"P.S. He's really good at it."

Does anyone have any color photos of Mike playing?  Didn't he play at the AstroBUG meeting in 1983?

19472: Since I've got some time off, I took Friday to go up to the University of Maryland's library and sift through some years of Weekly Television Digest With Consumer Electronics for video game-related coverage from 1980, 1981 and 1985. For the unfamiliar, WTD was a trade publication that covered the television and consumer electronics industries, and as such covered video games from pretty much the get-go. Anyway, I came across a few Bally Arcade related items that I figured I'd share, including Bally's search for a new owner of their consumer products line, Astrovision's pick-up, and a comment on estimated sales for 1981. Enjoy!

Thanks for posting these pictures of the Bally-related content, Kevin.  I love it when people use library resources for researching purposes.  I could not make out the date of one of the issues.  What is the month of this one:

Weekly Television Digest (1980 xx 29)(Vol. 30, No. 29) Page 15

I OCRed this piece of history from that issue of the trade magazine:

"Bally sold Consumer Products Div. to Astrovision of Columbus, O., newly formed for purpose of acquisition. Price wasn't disclosed. Vp Dan Dawson said Astrovision has already taken over marketing of Bally’s programmable video game, now listing at $299, plus library of 14 cartridges priced $20-$25. He said one new cartridge will be offered by year's end. Plans for 1981 include 6-8 new cartridges, add-on computer keyboard, export sales. Bally has been seeking buyer for consumer business for last 18 months, announced sale agreement with Fidelity Electronics last Jan., but deal fell through."

I didn't realize that the sale of the Bally system to Fidelity Electronics was anything more than a rumor.  It's really incredible that the Bally Arcade was able to make a sort-of-comeback from Astrocade, Inc. after being basically down-and-out for 1 1/2 years.

--------------------

Seeing...is trying.
Trying...is buying.

The Bally Professional Arcade practically sells itself in this eye-catching, custom P.O.P. Display. Passing shoppers can't resist it, and once they try their hand at the Bally "magic," they want to buy.

A specially prepared Demonstration Cassette gives potential buyers a 2-minute (approximately) overview of the Bally Arcade. It highlights some of the exclusive Bally features, and briefly shows the built-in games in action...GUNFIGHT, CHECKMATE and SCRIBBLING. It also lists optional Videocade Cassettes that are now available.

The Display unit includes space for the "pistol-grip" hand controls and the Arcade itself so that prospects can actually operate it and play the games as they would at home.

In addition, the Display has space for up to 188 cassettes plus add-on accessories. This pilfer-proof storage is all under lock and key.

Designed for maximum use of minimal space, the Display is also highly attractive and soundly constructed. It can be charged 100% to co-op accrual, and can be ordered [from Bally Consumer Products Division.]

One of the most advanced and powerful video game/home computer systems on the market. Built for superior performance today, and constantly expandable for tomorrow.

In addition to the 3 Arcade-Tested games already programmed into the Arcade unit, Videocade cassettes are also available in Action/Skill, Sports, Educational and Strategy series.

Bally Professional Arcade: The Home Computer with the Bally Brain.

----------
